diagnostics.meaning: The measured clearance does not justify further spacer adjustment.
diagnostics.next: Record the result; investigate any remaining cooling complaint separately.

verification.title: Record the final clearance
verification.body: Record the compressor type, specification used, final readings at all 3 positions and the tightening branch applied.

procedures.purpose: Clutch air-gap measurement and spacer adjustment, with separate fixed-compressor and EVDC tightening values.

guides.title: Inspect and replace the A/C compressor clutch and field coil
guides.summary: Remove the compressor clutch components, inspect their friction surfaces and bearing, and rebuild the assembly with the correct clutch air gap.
guides.introduction: The air-conditioning (A/C) compressor clutch connects the belt-driven pulley to the compressor shaft. Its stationary field coil creates the magnetic force that engages the clutch disc and hub. This job separates those parts so heat damage, worn contact surfaces and pulley-bearing roughness can be assessed directly. It applies to the fitted compressor hardware regardless of whether cabin temperature is controlled manually or automatically.
guides.why: Clutch construction determines how the hub is removed, while compressor type determines its tightening value. Keeping those distinctions clear prevents damage during dismantling. The final air gap—the clearance between the clutch contact surfaces—must also be measured and adjusted for correct engagement and release.

when.summary: When the compressor clutch, pulley bearing or field coil requires inspection or replacement.
notes: Identify both the clutch construction and compressor type before choosing the removal method and tightening value.

prepare.title: Arrange compressor removal
prepare.detail: This bench procedure begins with the compressor removed. Provide the A/C service capability and refrigerant-handling arrangements required by the fitted compressor's removal and installation procedure.

prepare.title: Have the correct holding and pulling tools
prepare.detail: Provide the universal clutch holding tool for a spring rubber clutch, suitable shaft-holding capability for a spring plate clutch, and compressor pulley remover 412-001. Have the clutch air-gap adjustment procedure and suitable measuring equipment ready.

prepare.title: Workshop capability
prepare.detail: A/C compressor with a spring rubber or spring plate clutch

steps.title: Remove the compressor and identify its branches
steps.body: Complete the applicable compressor removal procedure before beginning [clutch and field-coil service](#/document/G1890643). Identify the spring rubber or spring plate clutch, then identify whether the compressor is fixed or externally variable displacement (EVDC). These are separate choices in the procedure.

steps.title: Release the clutch hub correctly
steps.body: For a spring rubber clutch, hold the clutch with the universal holding tool and remove the disc-and-hub bolt. For a spring plate clutch, hold the compressor shaft and turn the hub counterclockwise to remove it. Use the method that matches the installed construction.

steps.title: Remove the pulley
steps.body: Remove the pulley snap ring, then use the specified pulley remover to withdraw the pulley. Do not use air tools: they can damage the clutch pulley or compressor.

steps.title: Remove the field coil
steps.body: Remove the field-coil electrical connector retainer, then remove the coil snap ring and field coil. This exposes the components for direct inspection.

steps.title: Inspect the separated components
steps.body: Examine the disc and hub, pulley and field coil for cracks, melting and heat discoloration. Check the clutch contact surfaces for grooves deeper than fingernail depth and assess the pulley bearing for roughness. Use these findings to identify which components require repair attention.

steps.title: Reassemble and adjust the air gap
steps.body: Reverse the dismantling sequence. Renew the applicable snap ring when installing a new component. Use the compressor-specific clutch fastening value: 20 Nm for the fixed compressor or 14.5 Nm for EVDC. Finally, measure and adjust the clutch air gap by adding or removing disc-and-hub spacers according to the separate air-gap adjustment procedure, then complete compressor installation.

watchFor.title: Heat damage extending beyond one part
watchFor.body: Inspect all three clutch components; a visibly damaged disc does not establish that the pulley and field coil are serviceable.

watchFor.title: An unchecked air gap
watchFor.body: Reassembly is incomplete until the gap has been measured and adjusted. Spacer selection cannot be replaced by estimating the clearance visually.

notes: The spring plate clutch uses the same final air-gap adjustment principle.
Use the specified air-gap value for the fitted compressor; no numerical gap is established in this procedure.

diagnostics.finding: Cracking, melting or heat discoloration.
diagnostics.meaning: The inspected component shows physical or thermal damage.
diagnostics.next: Assess the affected component for replacement and inspect the other clutch components.

diagnostics.finding: Contact-surface grooves deeper than fingernail depth.
diagnostics.meaning: The clutch disc/hub or pulley meets the stated excessive-wear criterion.
diagnostics.next: Address the worn component before rebuilding.

diagnostics.finding: Roughness in the pulley bearing.
diagnostics.meaning: The pulley bearing has an adverse mechanical inspection finding.
diagnostics.next: Resolve the bearing condition before final assembly.

verification.title: Confirm the assembly checks
verification.body: Confirm that the electrical connector retainer and snap rings have been restored and the correct compressor fastening branch was used.

verification.title: Record the final air gap
verification.body: Record the measured gap and any spacer adjustment, confirming compliance with the applicable clutch air-gap procedure.

procedures.purpose: Clutch-type-specific dismantling, pulley and field-coil inspection, reverse assembly and the required air-gap adjustment handoff.

guides.title: Check the 5.2L A/C compressor shaft for refrigerant leaks
guides.summary: Isolate and charge the A/C compressor for an electronic shaft-leak test, recover the test refrigerant and replace the compressor if an external leak is found.
guides.introduction: The air-conditioning compressor circulates refrigerant so the climate system can cool and dehumidify cabin air. This procedure checks for refrigerant escaping externally at the compressor shaft. It requires recovering the vehicle's refrigerant, disconnecting the compressor lines and connecting a service unit directly through adapters. The result determines whether an external compressor leak justifies fitting a new compressor.
guides.why: Recovering refrigerant before opening the lines allows controlled disconnection. Testing the isolated compressor uses a defined charge and a detector suited to R-134a, giving a focused check at the shaft. The test charge is for this operation only; it is not a specification for recharging the entire vehicle. Refrigerant must also be recovered from the compressor when the test ends.

when.summary: When checking the A/C compressor shaft for a suspected external refrigerant leak.
notes: The test applies to the compressor; it does not establish the condition of every other A/C component.

prepare.title: Provide refrigerant-service capability
prepare.detail: Use an air-conditioning service unit capable of recovery and charging, operated by someone competent in refrigerant handling. Have the applicable Group 412 recovery and compressor-line procedures available.

prepare.title: Have compatible compressor adapters
prepare.detail: Use the compressor-port adapters identified in the leak-detection procedure's A/C Flush Adapter Kit listings. The adapters attach with the existing retaining bolts.

prepare.title: Select the specified detector
prepare.detail: Use a Rotunda-approved electronic leak detector for R-134a refrigerant, SAE certified to J2791.

steps.title: Recover refrigerant from the vehicle
steps.body: Follow the Air Conditioning System Recovery, Evacuation and Charging procedure in Group 412. Complete recovery before opening the compressor connections.

steps.title: Disconnect the compressor lines
steps.body: Disconnect the refrigerant lines using the applicable Group 412 procedure. This prepares the compressor ports for the direct test connections.

steps.title: Fit adapters and service hoses
steps.body: Install the specified flush-kit adapters on the compressor ports with the existing retaining bolts. Connect the service unit's high- and low-pressure hoses to the corresponding adapter fittings.

steps.title: Apply the compressor test charge
steps.body: Follow the service unit's operating instructions. Open both its low- and high-pressure valves and set the refrigerant charge amount to 0.23 kg (8 oz). Charge the compressor for the leak test.

steps.title: Check the shaft for leakage
steps.body: Use the approved electronic detector to check for refrigerant leaks at the compressor shaft. Keep the finding specific to the location tested so it supports the correct repair decision.

steps.title: Recover the test refrigerant and decide the repair
steps.body: When testing is complete, recover refrigerant from the compressor regardless of the result. If an external leak is found, install a new A/C compressor using the applicable replacement procedure.

watchFor.title: Confusing test charge with vehicle capacity
watchFor.body: The 0.23 kg (8 oz) quantity belongs to the isolated-compressor test. Use the applicable charging procedure for the completed vehicle system.

watchFor.title: Stopping before recovery
watchFor.body: A completed detector check does not finish the operation until the compressor's test refrigerant has been recovered.

notes: Plan the applicable line or compressor installation and system evacuation/charging work before returning the A/C system to service.

diagnostics.finding: An external compressor leak is detected.
diagnostics.meaning: The test supports compressor replacement.
diagnostics.next: Recover the test refrigerant and install a new compressor.

diagnostics.finding: No shaft leak is detected during this test.
diagnostics.meaning: This check has not established an external shaft leak; it does not prove the whole A/C system is leak-free.
diagnostics.next: Recover the test refrigerant and continue diagnosis according to the original complaint.

verification.title: Confirm test closure
verification.body: Confirm that refrigerant has been recovered from the compressor after testing.

verification.title: Record the result and decision
verification.body: Record whether leakage was detected at the shaft and whether the finding requires compressor replacement.

procedures.purpose: Complete 5.2L compressor leak-detection setup, test charging, shaft inspection, refrigerant recovery and replacement decision.

guides.title: Treat musty air-conditioning odor on the 5.2L Mustang
guides.summary: Identify the odor source, correct moisture problems, and treat the evaporator only when the odor originates inside the air-conditioning system.
guides.introduction: Air conditioning (A/C) cools cabin air and reduces its humidity. Warmth and moisture can also support microbial growth around the evaporator and nearby materials. This job first separates that problem from leaks, outside smells and damp interior trim, then dries and coats the evaporator when treatment is justified.
guides.why: A smell that becomes stronger with the blower running does not necessarily originate in the evaporator. Treating wet carpeting or a fluid leak with cooling-coil coating leaves the cause untouched. Correct drainage, thorough drying and protection of electrical components matter as much as applying the approved product.

when.summary: When a musty startup odor has been traced to the A/C system after checking for leaks and other odor sources.
notes: Microbiological odors are not present at or below 10° C (50° F); consider the temperature when assessing the complaint.

prepare.title: Treatment equipment and access
prepare.detail: Have an A/C Odor Remover Flexible Applicator, one full bottle of Motorcraft® A/C Cooling Coil Coating YN-29, and the applicable blower motor removal and installation procedure.

prepare.title: Drying and cleanup
prepare.detail: Arrange suitable ventilation for extended engine running with the doors and windows open. A wet/dry vacuum can remove accessible standing water and debris at the cowl inlet.

steps.title: Establish the odor pattern
steps.body: Note when the smell starts, how long it lasts and whether fresh or recirculated air changes it. Use the distinctions below and the [odor inspection procedure](#/document/G1912355). Stop the A/C treatment path if the source is outside the system.

steps.title: Check drainage and water entry
steps.body: Check the evaporator drain tube for restriction. Inspect both front carpets, the blower motor and its cover, if equipped, for moisture. Wet carpets or blower components require water-leak diagnosis instead of odor treatment. Check the cowl panel and inlet screen for standing water or foreign material; remove water and clean the screen where possible.

steps.title: Dry the system
steps.body: Open all doors and windows. Keep A/C off, select REGISTER mode, set full warm and set the blower to HI. Run the engine for 25 minutes, then turn the ignition OFF. This prepares the evaporator for coating.

steps.title: Expose the evaporator safely
steps.body: Remove the blower motor using its applicable procedure. Remove the blower speed control or resistor if equipped and exposed inside the evaporator housing. A control mounted outside the housing and outside blower airflow does not require removal.

steps.title: Apply the approved coating
steps.body: Load the applicator with one full bottle of YN-29. Insert its nozzle into the evaporator housing and direct the spray toward the core face. Cover the entire face until the applicator is empty, keeping product off interior surfaces and the blower speed control.

steps.title: Reassemble and cure
steps.body: Reinstall the blower motor and any removed speed control or resistor. Repeat the open-door and open-window drying setup, with A/C off, REGISTER mode, full warm, blower HI and a 25-minute engine run, to cure the coating.

watchFor.title: Similar smells can have different causes
watchFor.body: Dust may smell musty, while evaporator coating can smell like wet cement. Odor description alone is insufficient.

watchFor.title: Use only the approved coating
watchFor.body: Other coatings can damage the factory coating and create further odor problems.

notes: Microbial growth can occur on seals, adhesives, soaked trim and standing water. Remove the source and let affected areas drain and dry.

diagnostics.finding: A largely constant chemical smell, sometimes stronger with A/C operation.
diagnostics.meaning: Fluid leaks or incorrectly cured adhesives may be responsible; coolant, fuel and oils have different characteristic smells.
diagnostics.next: Locate and repair the source and remove residue.

diagnostics.finding: A brief smell associated with an outside area, open windows or fresh-air operation.
diagnostics.meaning: An environmental source is likely.
diagnostics.next: Recirculation may reduce exposure; evaporator treatment cannot remove the outside source.

diagnostics.finding: Odor follows clothing, food, fragrance or another interior source.
diagnostics.meaning: The source may remain in the cabin and linger after removal.
diagnostics.next: Remove it and clean the affected area.

diagnostics.finding: Mustiness lasts about 30 seconds after A/C startup with either air setting.
diagnostics.meaning: This is consistent with an A/C microbial source; persistent mustiness, especially on recirculation, suggests another damp area.
diagnostics.next: Complete the moisture inspections before selecting treatment.

verification.title: Confirm treatment completion
verification.body: Check that removed components are installed and the curing run is complete before reassessing the original odor conditions.

verification.title: Record the result
verification.body: Record the original odor pattern, moisture findings, action taken and whether the odor remains.

procedures.purpose: 5.2L A/C odor classification, moisture inspection, evaporator drying, coating application and curing.

guides.title: Flush contaminated A/C condenser and evaporator cores
guides.summary: Back-flush contaminated air-conditioning heat exchangers, purge the cleaning solvent, and restore the system through the appropriate compressor repair branch.
guides.introduction: The air-conditioning (A/C) condenser releases heat, while the evaporator absorbs cabin heat and helps remove moisture from the air. Compressor or desiccant failure can leave debris inside these heat exchangers. This job cleans their internal passages before the refrigerant circuit returns to service.
guides.why: Flushing reverses normal refrigerant flow and filters debris from the returning solvent. Purging then removes that solvent: leaving cleaning fluid behind can damage the operating system. Components that trap debris or solvent must be removed from the flushing path.

when.summary: When compressor or desiccant failure leaves particles, or compressor seizure leaves gummy oil residue in the heat exchangers.

prepare.title: Arrange refrigerant-service capability
prepare.detail: Have refrigerant identification, recovery, oil servicing, evacuation, leak-testing and charging equipment available, with the applicable procedures and operating instructions.

prepare.title: Use the approved cleaning equipment
prepare.detail: Use only the Ford-approved A/C Flush and Purge Service Unit, matching A/C Adaptor Kit, Motorcraft A/C System Flushing Solvent (YN-23), and FL1-A filter. Read the unit instructions before first use.

steps.title: Identify and recover the refrigerant
steps.body: Identify refrigerant before recovery to protect the shop’s bulk supply. If contaminated, refer the customer to the last servicing facility, or use dedicated contaminated-refrigerant recovery equipment if the customer accepts the additional cost. Handle contaminated refrigerant as hazardous waste under applicable regulations. Follow the A/C System Recovery, Evacuation and Charging procedure referenced by the [flushing procedure](#/document/G1912322).

steps.title: Isolate the heat exchangers
steps.body: After recovery, disconnect the condenser and/or evaporator refrigerant lines using the applicable procedure. Remove the receiver drier or drier element, front thermostatic expansion valve (TXV), rear TXV if equipped, and hoses with mufflers. Do not flush through these components, including a condenser-integrated drier element.

steps.title: Back-flush each selected core
steps.body: Connect the service unit with the correct adapters so solvent travels opposite normal refrigerant flow. Use 3.78 L (1 gal) of YN-23 and flush each heat exchanger for a minimum of 15 minutes. The unit filters returning solvent before recirculation.

steps.title: Purge the solvent completely
steps.body: Supply air at 621-862 kPa (90-125 psi) through the service unit and purge each flushed component for a minimum of 30 minutes. This forces out and evaporates residual solvent. Dispose of used solvent and the filter according to local, state and federal regulations.

steps.title: Replace contamination-sensitive parts and reconnect
steps.body: For internal compressor or desiccant failure, install new fitted TXVs, refrigerant hoses with mufflers, and the receiver drier or drier element. Reconnect the serviced heat exchangers using their applicable installation procedures.

steps.title: Follow the correct compressor branch
steps.body: If retaining the compressor, add the correct amount of clean polyalkylene glycol (PAG) oil using the applicable Refrigerant Oil Adding procedure, then evacuate, leak test and charge. If installing a new compressor, continue with its installation procedure. Obtain the required oil amount and remaining completion instructions from that branch rather than assuming the retained-compressor sequence applies.

watchFor.title: Direct shop air
watchFor.body: Never blow shop air directly through the A/C circuit; the service unit must clean and dry it first.

watchFor.title: Solvent retention
watchFor.body: An incomplete purge can leave damaging solvent inside the core. Do not shorten the required purge.

notes: The solvent charge and filter may serve both heat exchangers on one vehicle, but must never be reused on another vehicle.
Removed driers, TXVs and muffler-equipped hoses are typically discarded after system contamination.

diagnostics.finding: Particles or gummy residue inside the heat exchangers
diagnostics.meaning: These are supported flushing targets, not by themselves a diagnosis of the original failure.
diagnostics.next: Establish the failure and apply its replacement requirements.

diagnostics.finding: A hose without a muffler contains foreign material
diagnostics.meaning: Reuse depends on whether it is clogged.
diagnostics.next: Reuse only if it is not clogged.

verification.title: Confirm the completion branch
verification.body: For a retained compressor, confirm oil servicing, evacuation, leak testing and charging are complete. For a replacement, follow its installation completion requirements.

verification.title: Record the cleaning result
verification.body: Record which cores were flushed, flushing and purge durations, replaced components, and the leak-test result when performed.

procedures.purpose: Complete condenser/evaporator flushing, purging, contamination-related replacement requirements, and retained-versus-new compressor completion branches.

applicability.equipment: A/C condenser and evaporator heat exchangers; manual or dual automatic climate control.

guides.title: Recover, evacuate and recharge the air-conditioning system
guides.summary: Identify and recover the refrigerant, complete the repair, then evacuate and recharge the circuit with controlled oil replacement.
guides.introduction: Air conditioning cools cabin air and reduces its humidity, whether the vehicle uses manual or automatic temperature control. Opening the refrigerant circuit requires a controlled service process: recovery captures the existing refrigerant, evacuation draws air and moisture from the repaired circuit, and charging restores the specified refrigerant quantity.
guides.why: Refrigerant purity must be established before recovery to protect the workshop's bulk supply. Both service ports are required because system solenoid valves can prevent complete recovery through the low side alone. Oil removed during recovery must also be accounted for so the repaired system receives the correct lubricant amount.

when.summary: When refrigerant-circuit repairs require recovery, followed by evacuation and a measured recharge.
notes: Establish the required repair before beginning; refrigerant service alone does not identify a failed component.

prepare.title: Use refrigerant-service equipment
prepare.detail: This work requires refrigerant-handling capability, identification equipment and Ford-approved R134a refrigerant management equipment. Follow the equipment manufacturer's connection and operating instructions.

prepare.title: Obtain charge and oil requirements
prepare.detail: Have the applicable refrigerant charge quantity and Refrigerant Oil Adding procedure available. Prepare the correct clean polyalkylene glycol (PAG) oil and a record of oil removed during recovery.

steps.title: Identify the refrigerant
steps.body: Analyze refrigerant purity before recovering any of it. If contaminated, arrange referral to the facility that last serviced the system, or obtain agreement for the additional cost of recovery using equipment dedicated to contaminated refrigerant. Keep contaminated material out of the normal recovery supply.

steps.title: Recover through both service ports
steps.body: Connect the service unit to the low-side and high-side ports and recover according to its instructions. Record any oil removed. Let the system stand for about 2 minutes and observe the vacuum. If it is lost, repeat recovery and the observation period until the vacuum remains stable for 2 minutes, then disconnect the equipment.

steps.title: Complete the required repair
steps.body: Carry out the refrigerant-system repair after recovery is complete. Retain the measured oil-loss figure: that amount must be replaced after repairs, using the applicable oil-adding procedure.

steps.title: Evacuate the repaired circuit
steps.body: Connect the equipment to both service ports. Draw at least 99.4 kPa (29.5 in-Hg) of vacuum, as close to 101.1 kPa (30 in-Hg) as possible. Continue operating the vacuum pump for a minimum of 45 minutes. Analyze the refrigerant again before any additional recovery operation.

steps.title: Check vacuum retention
steps.body: Switch off the vacuum pump and observe the low-pressure gauge for 10 minutes. The system must hold vacuum. If the reading falls, resolve the failure to hold vacuum before proceeding; this observation does not identify the location of a leak.

steps.title: Restore oil and charge
steps.body: Use the applicable oil-adding procedure to provide the correct amount of clean PAG oil, accounting for the oil removed during recovery. Follow the [charging procedure](#/document/G1912323), connect both service ports as required, set the specified refrigerant charge amount and complete charging according to the service-unit instructions.

watchFor.title: Contaminated refrigerant
watchFor.body: Use dedicated recovery equipment when that option is chosen. Dispose of contaminated refrigerant as hazardous waste under applicable federal, state and local requirements.

watchFor.title: Incomplete recovery
watchFor.body: A low-side-only connection cannot be used as a substitute for connecting both service ports.

notes: The listed analyzer supports R134a and R1234yf identification; this procedure specifies Ford-approved R134a refrigerant management equipment.

diagnostics.finding: Vacuum is lost during the recovery settling period.
diagnostics.meaning: The recovery completion condition has not been met.
diagnostics.next: Repeat recovery and observation until vacuum remains stable for 2 minutes.

diagnostics.finding: Vacuum falls during the post-evacuation observation.
diagnostics.meaning: The repaired circuit has not passed the vacuum-hold check.
diagnostics.next: Investigate and resolve the loss before charging.

verification.title: Confirm evacuation completion
verification.body: Confirm the specified vacuum level, minimum pump-running period and successful 10-minute hold.

verification.title: Record the service quantities
verification.body: Record refrigerant identification, oil removed and replaced, and the charge quantity set on the service unit.

procedures.purpose: Complete refrigerant identification prerequisites, recovery, evacuation, vacuum-hold checking and charging.

guides.title: Check the A/C condenser core for a refrigerant leak
guides.summary: Isolate and evacuate the condenser, then distinguish a genuine vacuum loss from leaking test connections or refrigerant outgassing.
guides.introduction: The air-conditioning condenser releases heat from the refrigerant as part of the system that cools and dehumidifies cabin air. This check disconnects the condenser from the rest of the system and tests its ability to hold a vacuum. It establishes whether the core leaks before replacement is justified.
guides.why: Refrigerant can remain dissolved in oil inside the condenser. Under vacuum it escapes from the oil and can make the gauge appear to show a leak. The extended evacuation removes that source of error, while checking hose valves and adapters ensures the test actually reaches the condenser.

when.summary: When condenser leakage is suspected and an isolated core test is needed.
notes: A cooling complaint alone does not establish that the condenser leaks.

prepare.title: Arrange refrigerant-service capability
prepare.detail: Use an air-conditioning service unit and the correct condenser adapter fittings from the specified adapter kits. Refrigerant recovery and condenser disconnection require the applicable Group 412 procedures.

prepare.title: Allow enough observation time
prepare.detail: The initial evacuation includes at least 45 minutes after reaching the specified vacuum. Small-leak investigation can require additional evacuation, observation and an overnight hold.

steps.title: Recover refrigerant and isolate the condenser
steps.body: Recover the refrigerant through the referenced A/C System Recovery, Evacuation and Charging procedure before disconnecting the condenser. Follow the applicable condenser access procedure.

steps.title: Connect a valid test circuit
steps.body: Fit the correct adapters and connect the service-unit hoses. Prefer hoses without automatic shut-off valves where available. If shut-off valves are present, confirm that the adapters open them; otherwise the test is invalid.

steps.title: Evacuate long enough to remove trapped refrigerant
steps.body: Open both valves and start the vacuum. Once the low-pressure gauge indicates 101 kPa (30 in-Hg) of vacuum, continue for at least 45 minutes. If that indication cannot be reached, follow the large-leak decision below.

steps.title: Observe the isolated vacuum
steps.body: After the full evacuation period, close the valves and stop the service unit. The gauge should remain at 101 kPa (30 in-Hg). Observe its movement over the specified test period rather than judging a momentary reading.

steps.title: Resolve a possible small leak
steps.body: If a very small leak is suspected, observe for 30 minutes. For a small vacuum loss, run the service unit with the valves open for another 30 minutes to remove remaining refrigerant from the oil, then recheck. If necessary, leave the isolated condenser under vacuum overnight and inspect for loss.

steps.title: Make the replacement decision
steps.body: Replace the condenser only when leakage is verified by the [Condenser Core Leak Check](#/document/G1912324). Use the referenced Group 412 Condenser procedure for replacement and the applicable refrigerant-service procedure for return to service.

watchFor.title: A hose valve that stays closed
watchFor.body: A closed valve can isolate the condenser from the test equipment and produce a misleading result.

watchFor.title: Outgassing mistaken for leakage
watchFor.body: Do not shorten the evacuation period. Small vacuum losses require the additional evacuation and recheck before a conclusion.

notes: This isolated test assesses the condenser; it does not locate leaks elsewhere in the air-conditioning system.

diagnostics.finding: The target vacuum cannot be reached, and the reading rises rapidly to zero after closing the valves.
diagnostics.meaning: A large leak is indicated, but an adapter connection may be responsible.
diagnostics.next: Recheck the adapter fittings before installing a new condenser.

diagnostics.finding: Vacuum is lost by 34 kPa (10 in-Hg) or more from the target indication in 10 minutes.
diagnostics.meaning: The specified leak criterion has been met.
diagnostics.next: With the test connections verified, follow the condenser replacement procedure.

verification.title: Confirm test validity
verification.body: Confirm that the condenser was connected through open hose valves and received the full evacuation period after reaching the target indication.

verification.title: Record the gauge result
verification.body: Record the starting vacuum, elapsed observation time, vacuum loss and any additional evacuation or overnight result supporting the decision.

procedures.purpose: Isolated condenser vacuum testing, adapter and hose requirements, outgassing control, leak criteria and replacement decision.

guides.title: Locate an R-134a air-conditioning leak electronically
guides.summary: Check service ports and refrigerant-system components with an approved electronic detector while controlling contamination and test conditions.
guides.introduction: The air-conditioning refrigerant circuit supports cabin cooling and moisture removal. An electronic leak detector senses refrigerant escaping around a fitting, line or component and helps locate the area needing further attention. This procedure is for R-134a. It establishes a leak-search method; an alarm must be interpreted in relation to the surrounding air and the position of the detector tip.
guides.why: A detector can respond to refrigerant already present in the workshop or trapped around a service port. Antifreeze, brake cleaner and other cleaning solvents can also interfere. R-134a tends to move downward because it is heavier than air, so searching only above a connection can miss a leak. Clean test conditions and thorough coverage make the findings more useful.

when.summary: When an R-134a refrigerant leak needs locating during an air-conditioning investigation.
notes: Use the stated engine and temperature conditions when interpreting system pressure.
Detector response in contaminated air does not reliably locate an individual leak.

prepare.title: Use the specified detector capability
prepare.detail: Use a Rotunda-approved electronic detector for R-134a that is SAE certified to J2791. The procedure lists a Robinair infrared refrigerant detector. Follow the detector's own handling and operating instructions.

prepare.title: Arrange a suitable test environment
prepare.detail: Provide good ventilation and access around the refrigerant lines, fittings and components. A fan may clear contamination before testing, but turn it off during the actual search.

prepare.title: Arrange pressure assessment
prepare.detail: The operator needs the capability to check A/C system pressure and interpret it with the engine off and cool. A hot engine can produce a higher pressure reading.

steps.title: Clear the surrounding air
steps.body: Ventilate the test area before using the detector. Remove lingering refrigerant or chemical contamination from the air as far as practical, then stop any ventilation fan used for this preparation before taking leak readings.

steps.title: Prepare and test the service ports
steps.body: Remove the service-port caps and blow air over the ports to clear trapped refrigerant before checking them. This preparation helps distinguish a port-area leak indication from refrigerant left beneath a cap.

steps.title: Assess the pressure conditions
steps.body: The [electronic leak-detection procedure](#/document/G1912325) states a system pressure of 413-551 kPa (60 - 80 psi) at 24° C (75.2° F), with the engine off and cool. Account for engine heat when interpreting a higher reading.

steps.title: Search the refrigerant circuit thoroughly
steps.body: Test around the fittings, lines and components using the detector manufacturer's operating technique. Pass the sensing tip below, above and around each area; the downward movement of R-134a makes the lower side particularly easy to overlook.

steps.title: Separate local findings from background response
steps.body: If the detector indicates gas everywhere, reassess contamination before assigning a leak location. Record localized responses together with the test conditions so the next repair decision follows the observed finding.

watchFor.title: A fan running during the search
watchFor.body: The procedure permits a fan to clear the area beforehand but requires it to be off during actual testing.

watchFor.title: Incomplete coverage
watchFor.body: A quiet detector above a fitting does not complete the check. Test its underside and surrounding area as well.

notes: Use the detector's operating instructions for technique; no universal probe speed or alarm threshold is specified here.

diagnostics.finding: The detector responds continuously throughout the area.
diagnostics.meaning: Ambient refrigerant or interfering chemical odors may be affecting the readings.
diagnostics.next: Ventilate before testing again, then switch the fan off for the search.

diagnostics.finding: A service port indicates refrigerant before trapped gas has been cleared.
diagnostics.meaning: Gas beneath the cap can obscure whether the port is leaking.
diagnostics.next: Blow air over the uncapped port as directed, then perform the leak check.

diagnostics.finding: Pressure is higher while the engine is hot.
diagnostics.meaning: Engine heat can raise the reading relative to the stated cool-engine condition.
diagnostics.next: Interpret the pressure against the specified temperature and engine state before drawing a conclusion.

verification.title: Confirm search quality
verification.body: Confirm that prepared service ports and the refrigerant circuit were checked with the fan off and with coverage below, above and around the inspected areas.

verification.title: Record the result
verification.body: Record the pressure, temperature and engine condition, along with localized indications or the absence of an indication in the areas checked. Note any contamination that limited interpretation.

procedures.purpose: R-134a electronic leak inspection, including approved detector requirements, ventilation, service-port preparation and pressure conditions.

guides.title: Test the A/C evaporator core for refrigerant leaks
guides.summary: Isolate and evacuate the evaporator, then assess vacuum loss while ruling out adapter leaks and refrigerant released from residual oil.
guides.introduction: The air conditioning (A/C) evaporator absorbs heat from cabin air and helps remove moisture during cooling. This test checks whether the isolated evaporator can retain vacuum before replacement is justified. It applies to the evaporator itself, regardless of whether cabin temperature is controlled manually or automatically.
guides.why: A falling vacuum can have several explanations. A leaking adapter can imitate a leaking core, while refrigerant remaining in evaporator oil can escape gradually and spoil the reading. Conversely, a closed hose shut-off valve can prevent the equipment from testing the evaporator at all. Correct connections and the full evacuation time make the result meaningful.

when.summary: When an evaporator refrigerant leak is suspected and needs confirmation before core replacement.
notes: Weak cooling alone does not identify the evaporator as the leaking component.

prepare.title: Provide refrigerant-service capability
prepare.detail: Use an air conditioning service unit and the correct evaporator adapter kit. Refrigerant recovery and evaporator disconnection require the applicable Group 412 procedures.

prepare.title: Check hose valve operation
prepare.detail: Prefer hoses without automatic shut-off valves where available. If shut-off valves are present, confirm they open when connected to the adapter fittings; otherwise the test is invalid.

steps.title: Recover refrigerant and isolate the core
steps.body: Recover the refrigerant using the applicable A/C recovery, evacuation and charging procedure. Disconnect the evaporator from the system using the appropriate Group 412 procedure.

steps.title: Connect the test equipment
steps.body: Fit the correct adapters to the evaporator and connect the service-unit hoses. Confirm any hose shut-off valves actually open at these fittings before beginning the [evaporator leak check](#/document/G1912326).

steps.title: Establish vacuum and assess a possible large leak
steps.body: Open both valves and start evacuation. If the low-pressure gauge cannot reach the specified vacuum mark of 101 kPa (30 in-Hg), close the valves and observe it. A rapid return to zero indicates a large leak; recheck adapter connections before condemning the core.

steps.title: Complete the timed evacuation and initial hold
steps.body: Once the gauge reaches the specified mark, continue evacuation for at least 45 minutes to remove refrigerant from residual oil. Close the valves and stop the unit. The gauge should hold at the vacuum mark. A loss of 34 kPa (10 in-Hg) or more within 10 minutes indicates a leak.

steps.title: Resolve a small or uncertain loss
steps.body: If a very small leak is suspected, observe the gauge after 30 minutes. If a small amount of vacuum is lost, reopen the valves and evacuate for an additional 30 minutes to remove remaining refrigerant from the oil, then repeat the hold check.

steps.title: Extend observation and make the repair decision
steps.body: For a suspected very small leak, leave vacuum applied overnight and check for loss. Install a new evaporator only when leakage is verified by this process, following the applicable Group 412 evaporator procedure.

watchFor.title: Timing started too early
watchFor.body: The minimum evacuation period starts after the gauge reaches the specified vacuum mark, not when the service unit first starts.

watchFor.title: Outgassing mistaken for leakage
watchFor.body: A small initial loss requires the additional evacuation and recheck branch before it is treated as confirmed core leakage.

notes: Keep the adapter and hose arrangement under consideration throughout the test; the gauge reflects the connected test volume.

diagnostics.finding: Vacuum cannot be established and rapidly returns to zero after valve closure.
diagnostics.meaning: A large leak is indicated, but an adapter connection may be responsible.
diagnostics.next: Recheck the adapter fittings before selecting evaporator replacement.

diagnostics.finding: Vacuum loss meets the specified 10-minute threshold after full evacuation.
diagnostics.meaning: The test indicates leakage.
diagnostics.next: Proceed to evaporator replacement once the test connections are established as sound.

diagnostics.finding: Only a small vacuum loss appears.
diagnostics.meaning: Residual refrigerant outgassing can resemble a very small leak.
diagnostics.next: Perform the additional evacuation, repeat the observation and use the overnight check when needed.

verification.title: Record the test result
verification.body: Record the starting vacuum, evacuation duration, elapsed hold times and observed loss, including any additional evacuation or overnight result.

verification.title: Document the resulting decision
verification.body: Distinguish a valid holding result, confirmed leakage and an invalid test caused by hose valves or connections. Base replacement on the verified leak result.

procedures.purpose: Isolated evaporator vacuum leak test, including equipment connections, timed observations and replacement criteria.

guides.title: Find and verify air-conditioning leaks with fluorescent dye
guides.summary: Use the factory-installed fluorescent dye to locate refrigerant leaks, clean repaired areas and check for fresh leakage.
guides.introduction: Air conditioning cools cabin air and reduces its relative humidity. A refrigerant leak can compromise that operation, but finding the escape point requires inspection. The factory-installed fluorescent dye helps because it adheres to the system oil: escaping refrigerant carries oil and dye through a leak, leaving a bright yellow-green trace under a suitable ultraviolet lamp.
guides.why: A glowing stain can identify a leak location, while old residue can confuse a post-repair check. The lamp also matters: not every ultraviolet lamp makes this dye fluoresce. A thorough inspection must cover the entire refrigerant circuit because more than one leak may exist.
searchTerms: AC leak not visible under UV

when.summary: When investigating suspected refrigerant leakage or verifying an air-conditioning leak repair.
notes: Weak cooling alone does not establish a refrigerant leak.
An empty system that has stood through winter may need a recharge and operation before residual dye becomes visible.

prepare.title: Use compatible detection equipment
prepare.detail: Prepare a Rotunda-approved ultraviolet (UV) leak-detection lamp and dye-enhancing glasses or goggles. A Rotunda-approved electronic leak detector is also useful for small leaks.

prepare.title: Plan cleanup and refrigerant work
prepare.detail: Have a general-purpose oil solvent for removing dye after repair. Any required recharge or component repair needs the appropriate refrigerant-service capability and its own operating procedure.

steps.title: Begin with the dye already in the system
steps.body: Follow the [fluorescent dye leak-detection procedure](#/document/G1912327). Do not add dye before diagnosis, after repairs or after flushing, even if a significant amount of refrigerant has been removed.

steps.title: Inspect the whole refrigerant circuit
steps.body: Use the approved UV lamp and dye-enhancing glasses to inspect every component, line and fitting. Look for the characteristic bright yellow-green trace. Continue around the circuit after finding one suspect location because additional leaks may be present.

steps.title: Account for oxidized dye
steps.body: If the system has been out of refrigerant through winter, dye at the leak may have oxidized and stopped fluorescing. In that circumstance, recharge and operate the air-conditioning system using the appropriate service procedure. Circulating oil can carry residual dye back to the escape point.

steps.title: Repair the leak and remove old traces
steps.body: Carry out the repair appropriate to each identified leak. After repair, remove fluorescent dye traces with a general-purpose oil solvent. Cleaning establishes a clear starting point for deciding whether dye subsequently returns.

steps.title: Operate and inspect again
steps.body: Run the vehicle for a short period and recheck the repaired area with the approved UV lamp. Fresh fluorescence at that location calls for further investigation rather than accepting the repair.

steps.title: Allow for small leaks
steps.body: Dye can take time to reappear at a small leak. Supplement the UV check with an approved electronic leak detector, following the Electronic Leak Detection procedure for its use.

watchFor.title: No fluorescence is not conclusive
watchFor.body: An unsuitable lamp, oxidized dye or a small leak can prevent an immediate visible indication.

watchFor.title: Unnecessary extra dye
watchFor.body: Replacement suction accumulators, receiver driers, receiver drier elements and service condensers contain a dye wafer in the desiccant bag. It dissolves after approximately 30 minutes of continuous air-conditioning operation.

notes: The dye guidance identifies the factory R-134a fluorescent-dye system; it is not a refrigerant charge specification.
Flushing does not justify adding dye because the flushing procedure includes a new accumulator, receiver drier or receiver drier element.

diagnostics.finding: Bright yellow-green dye is visible at a component, line or fitting.
diagnostics.meaning: The trace identifies a location to investigate for escaping refrigerant and oil.
diagnostics.next: Inspect the rest of the circuit, repair confirmed leaks and clean away dye before verification.

diagnostics.finding: A small suspected leak produces no immediate fresh dye.
diagnostics.meaning: The observation period may be too short for a visible trace.
diagnostics.next: Use electronic leak detection as an additional check.

verification.title: Check the cleaned repair area
verification.body: After brief vehicle operation, inspect again with the approved UV lamp and investigate any returning dye.

verification.title: Record the result
verification.body: Record the inspected leak locations, repairs, cleanup and whether fresh dye appeared during the recheck. Include any electronic-detector findings.

procedures.purpose: Fluorescent-dye inspection, no-additional-dye requirements, oxidized-dye handling and post-repair leak verification.

guides.title: Pressure-test the heater core for a coolant leak
guides.summary: Distinguish leakage at the heater hoses from leakage in the heater core using a water-filled pressure test.
guides.introduction: The heater core transfers heat from engine coolant into cabin air. Whether the vehicle uses Electronic Manual Temperature Control (EMTC) or Dual Automatic Temperature Control (DATC), coolant seen near the core does not automatically mean the core has failed. A leaking hose connection can allow coolant to follow the tube toward the core and create a misleading wet area.
guides.why: Checking the hose attachments first can prevent unnecessary core replacement. The pressure test then isolates the core and its temporary hose connections from the rest of the cooling system. A falling gauge reading becomes a replacement decision only after leakage at those hose connections has been excluded.

when.summary: When coolant leakage near the heater core or its hose attachments needs to be traced.
notes: The test establishes leakage; it is not a general test of cabin temperature-control operation.

prepare.title: Prepare cooling-system service
prepare.detail: Be equipped to drain and subsequently restore the cooling system using the applicable engine’s Cooling System Draining, Filling, and Bleeding procedure in Group 303.

prepare.title: Assemble the test equipment
prepare.detail: Use the 014-R1072 Radiator Pressure Test Set, plug 221373, adapter 221374, water, hose clamps and a short heater-hose section approximately 101 mm (4 in) long for each core tube.

steps.title: Inspect the existing hose attachments
steps.body: Look for coolant leakage where each heater hose joins the core tube. Check clamp integrity before attributing the wet area to the core. Original equipment uses spring-type clamps; nonspecified or overtightened clamps can cause leaks and damage.

steps.title: Drain and isolate the core
steps.body: Drain the cooling system through the applicable engine procedure, then disconnect the heater hoses from the core. This prepares the core for a separate test with its own controlled connections.

steps.title: Build the water-filled test arrangement
steps.body: Install a short hose section on each core tube. Fill the core and hoses with water, then install the test-kit plug and adapter. Secure the hoses, plug and adapter with hose clamps.

steps.title: Apply the specified pressure
steps.body: Connect the pump and gauge assembly to the adapter. Close the bleed valve at the base of the gauge, then pump 138 kPa (20 psi) of air pressure into the water-filled core.

steps.title: Observe the gauge
steps.body: Watch the pressure for a minimum of 3 minutes. Use the full observation period to determine whether pressure is retained rather than deciding from the initial reading alone.

steps.title: Locate any pressure loss
steps.body: If pressure falls, inspect the heater-hose connections at the core tubes for leakage. If those connections do not leak, replace the heater core. Account for any connection leakage before making the core replacement decision.

watchFor.title: Coolant following the tube
watchFor.body: A hose leak can appear to originate at the core because coolant travels along the tube.

watchFor.title: Clamp damage
watchFor.body: Do not use extra clamp force to compensate for an unsuitable connection; overtightening can damage the core.

notes: After testing or repair, complete cooling-system restoration through the applicable draining, filling and bleeding procedure. This test does not specify a shared coolant or refill quantity for every engine.

diagnostics.finding: Pressure falls and a heater-hose connection leaks.
diagnostics.meaning: The test has not isolated the core as the leak source.
diagnostics.next: Correct the leaking connection and repeat the pressure check.

diagnostics.finding: Pressure falls without leakage at the heater-hose connections.
diagnostics.meaning: The heater core meets the stated replacement criterion.
diagnostics.next: Replace the heater core.

diagnostics.finding: Pressure remains steady throughout the observation period.
diagnostics.meaning: No pressure loss was demonstrated under these test conditions.
diagnostics.next: Retain that result when assessing the original leakage evidence.

verification.title: Record the test result
verification.body: Record the starting and ending gauge readings, observation duration, hose-connection findings and resulting repair decision.

procedures.purpose: Heater-hose inspection, isolated heater-core pressure test and replacement decision.

applicability.equipment: Heater core on vehicles with electronic manual or dual automatic temperature control.

guides.title: Identify A/C refrigerant before recovery or charging
guides.summary: Test refrigerant composition before service to identify contamination and keep unsuitable refrigerant out of normal recovery equipment.
guides.introduction: Air conditioning cools cabin air and reduces its humidity. Before recovering refrigerant from the vehicle or charging it from a storage container, identification testing establishes what the refrigerant actually contains. This is a service decision point: a contaminated sample requires a different recovery route, while air in an otherwise pure sample has its own interpretation.
guides.why: Contaminated refrigerant can spoil the recovered refrigerant supply and damage recovery equipment. Air also affects A/C performance, but the identifier excludes air when calculating refrigerant purity. Understanding that distinction prevents a green purity result from being mistaken for confirmation that the sample contains no air.

when.summary: Before recovering or charging refrigerant, including refrigerant supplied from a storage container.
notes: The stated purity thresholds describe R-134a results; do not apply them automatically to R-1234yf.

prepare.title: Arrange suitable identification equipment
prepare.detail: Use refrigerant identification equipment conforming to SAE J1771 for R-134a, or equipment conforming to SAE J2912 that identifies R-134a and R-1234yf. Have its operating instructions available.

prepare.title: Prepare for a contamination finding
prepare.detail: The workshop must be able to arrange dedicated recovery-only equipment for contaminated refrigerant and follow the applicable A/C flushing procedure if contamination is confirmed.

steps.title: Sample the actual refrigerant source
steps.body: Take the sample directly from the vehicle refrigeration system or storage container, following the identifier manufacturer's sampling instructions. Sampling precedes recovery or charging so an unsuitable supply is recognized before it enters service equipment.

steps.title: Read composition alongside the indicator
steps.body: Use the result distinctions below and the complete [identification procedure](#/document/G1912329). The display reports the weight concentrations of R-134a, R-12, R-22 and hydrocarbons. Air content is displayed when the R-134a purity requirement is met.

steps.title: Verify an apparent contamination result
steps.body: Repeat the identification test whenever contaminated refrigerant is detected. This establishes whether the contamination finding is repeatable before the workshop proceeds with the contaminated-refrigerant recovery route.

steps.title: Keep confirmed contamination isolated
steps.body: Do not recover contaminated refrigerant into R-134a recovery/recycling equipment. Use recovery-only equipment specifically designed to capture and store contaminated refrigerant, protecting both the normal recovered supply and the recycling equipment.

steps.title: Correct the original concern and complete follow-on work
steps.body: Determine and correct the customer's initial concern, then follow Air Conditioning (A/C) System Flushing in Group 412. Replace the suction accumulator, receiver drier or receiver drier element as that procedure directs. Dispose of contaminated refrigerant according to applicable federal, state and local regulations.

watchFor.title: Hazard alarms
watchFor.body: A red failure indication and audible alarm require attention to the reported composition, especially a Hydrocarbon High message.

watchFor.title: A purity pass with air present
watchFor.body: Air is excluded from the refrigerant purity calculation, so a passing result does not establish that air content is acceptable.

notes: Sampling and any offered air-purge operation remain subject to the identification equipment's instructions.

diagnostics.finding: R-134a purity is 98% or greater by weight.
diagnostics.meaning: The green PASS indicator confirms the specified refrigerant purity threshold.
diagnostics.next: Review the displayed air content before continuing refrigerant service.

diagnostics.finding: R-134a purity is below 98% by weight.
diagnostics.meaning: The red FAIL indicator and alarm identify a sample that does not meet the purity requirement.
diagnostics.next: Repeat the identification test; confirmed contamination requires dedicated recovery-only equipment.

diagnostics.finding: Hydrocarbons are 2% or greater by weight.
diagnostics.meaning: The identifier reports Hydrocarbon High, illuminates FAIL and sounds an alarm for potential hazards.
diagnostics.next: Verify the result by repeating the test and keep confirmed contaminated refrigerant out of normal recovery/recycling equipment.

diagnostics.finding: R-134a purity passes and air is 2% or greater by weight.
diagnostics.meaning: The identifier offers an air purge; the air has not caused the refrigerant purity calculation to fail.
diagnostics.next: Respond to the purge prompt according to the equipment instructions.

verification.title: Record the identification result
verification.body: Record the sampled source, indicated composition, pass/fail result and any repeated contamination result so the subsequent service route is traceable.

verification.title: Confirm the correct recovery route
verification.body: For confirmed contamination, verify dedicated recovery was used and that flushing-related component replacement and disposal requirements were addressed.

procedures.purpose: Refrigerant sampling, R-134a result interpretation, repeat testing and the confirmed-contamination recovery pathway.

guides.title: Balance and add A/C refrigerant oil after repairs
guides.summary: Restore the refrigerant oil lost during component replacement or leak repair using the correct allowance and compressor-specific balancing method.
guides.introduction: Air-conditioning refrigerant carries lubricating oil around the system, leaving some oil inside each component. Removing a component therefore removes part of the oil supply. This job restores that loss; compressor replacement also requires attention because a new service compressor arrives containing a full system oil charge.
guides.why: The aim is to preserve the original total oil quantity. Adding a fully charged compressor to oil already elsewhere in the system can upset that balance. Use only clean, new Motorcraft PAG Refrigerant Compressor Oil YN-12-D; other oils can damage the compressor and contaminate the system.

when.summary: After refrigerant component replacement or leak repair, when lost oil must be restored.
notes: Balance replacement-compressor oil whenever the system will not be flushed.
Identify the actual compressor design before choosing its draining method.

prepare.title: Arrange refrigerant-service equipment
prepare.detail: Use an A/C service unit, refrigerant analyzer, oil injector set and clean measuring container. Follow equipment instructions, including the injector manufacturer's first-use instructions.

prepare.title: Prepare clean materials
prepare.detail: Keep equipment free of foreign material. Have YN-12-D oil available and establish the applicable component allowance before filling the injector.

steps.title: Analyze refrigerant before recovery
steps.body: Use the analyzer before connecting refrigerant to the recovery supply, and measure oil collected during recovery. Contaminated refrigerant requires referral to the previous servicing facility or an authorized service using dedicated contaminated-refrigerant recovery equipment. Dispose of contaminated refrigerant as hazardous waste.

steps.title: Select the repair allowance
steps.body: Use the chart in [Refrigerant Oil Adding](#/document/G1912330). Add the recovered oil quantity to these allowances: receiver drier, 60 ml; drier element, 30 ml; condenser, 45 ml; condenser with drier element, 60 ml; evaporator, 45 ml; hose or line, 60 ml; O-ring repair, 30 ml. The O-ring allowance applies once, even for several repaired leaks. Expansion-valve installation/reassembly and service-port repairs require only the recovered quantity. Compressor replacement requires oil matching plus the recovered quantity.

steps.title: Balance Type 1 or Type 3 compressors
steps.body: Type 1 is internally variable displacement; Type 3 is externally variable displacement. Drain the old compressor through its drain-bolt opening while turning its clutch 6 to 8 revolutions, ensuring the shaft turns. Refit its drain bolt. Uncap and drain the new compressor the same way, then refill it with clean oil equal to the old compressor's measured amount. Refit the new drain bolt to the type-specific torque and replace the port cap.

steps.title: Use the separate Type 2 method
steps.body: For this externally variable displacement design, remove the clutch and field coil from both compressors using their applicable procedures. Remove the drain bolts and press the suction damper to ventilate each compressor while draining; remove the new compressor's suction cap first. Close the old drain opening, refill the new compressor to match the measured old quantity, then refit its drain bolt, suction cap, clutch and field coil.

steps.title: Balance a Type 4 fixed compressor
steps.body: Collect oil through the discharge port while turning the old compressor clutch 6 to 8 revolutions. Uncap the new compressor, tilt it and drain through its discharge port while rotating likewise. Ensure the shafts turn. Add clean oil matching the old quantity and replace the new compressor's port cap.

steps.title: Choose the specified filling route
steps.body: During charging, inject the calculated allowance through the low-side service port. The chart also permits direct inlet-port addition for the condenser, condenser with drier element, and evaporator. Use the applicable method once for the calculated dose.

steps.title: Use the injector-set operating sequence when applicable
steps.body: With the engine off and cool, system pressure should be 413–551 kPa at 24°C. Fill and adjust the injector, then connect it to the low-side service valve. Clear every hose and tool from the cooling fan and drive belt before starting the engine. Switch A/C on and turn the injector piston clockwise to deliver the oil.

watchFor.title: Pulley rotation without shaft rotation
watchFor.body: For the rotating-drain methods, turning only the pulley will not satisfy the draining instruction.

watchFor.title: Different drain-bolt specifications
watchFor.body: Types 1, 2 and 3 have different drain-bolt tightening values. Use the identified type's instructions.

notes: Factory fluorescent dye normally makes additional dye unnecessary before leak diagnosis, even after substantial refrigerant removal.

Replacement receiver driers and elements contain a dye wafer that dissolves after approximately 30 minutes of continuous A/C operation. Additional dye is unnecessary after flushing when the prescribed new desiccant component is installed.

diagnostics.finding: Excessive oil escaped through a ruptured or separated hose or other damage.
diagnostics.meaning: The ordinary component allowance does not cover this loss.
diagnostics.next: Replace the receiver drier and follow the total-system-oil-capacity branch, establishing the vehicle's specified capacity before filling.

verification.title: Record the oil balance
verification.body: Record recovered oil, old-compressor drain quantity when applicable, the repair allowance and the amount delivered.

verification.title: Confirm branch completion
verification.body: Check that applicable drain bolts, port caps, clutch and field coil have been restored according to the selected compressor procedure.

procedures.purpose: Complete component oil allowances, compressor-type balancing, service-unit filling and injector-set procedure.

guides.title: Check A/C operating pressures on the 5.2L Mustang
guides.summary: Measure stabilized refrigerant pressures under controlled conditions to distinguish airflow, charge, restriction and compressor concerns.
guides.introduction: The air-conditioning compressor circulates refrigerant through a low-pressure suction side and a high-pressure discharge side. Comparing both pressures helps explain poor cooling, but only when temperature, airflow and control settings are consistent. This test applies to the 5.2L system and accommodates either manual or dual automatic temperature controls.
guides.why: Ambient temperature and condenser airflow affect operating pressures. A reading taken before pressures settle can suggest the wrong fault. Variable-compressor diagnosis also depends on the correct refrigerant charge, so pressure results alone must not lead straight to compressor replacement.
searchTerms: refrigerant high and low pressure test

when.summary: When investigating inadequate cooling or abnormal compressor operation in sufficiently warm ambient conditions.
notes: Testing requires ambient temperature of at least 21°C (70°F).
The supplied chart ranges extend to 49°C (120°F); do not extrapolate beyond the applicable chart.

prepare.title: Arrange refrigerant-service capability
prepare.detail: Use an air-conditioning service unit and someone capable of connecting and operating it correctly. Variable-compressor assessment may also require refrigerant recovery and recharging to the vehicle specification.

prepare.title: Select the correct charts
prepare.detail: Use the paired suction and discharge charts for 21–38°C (70–100°F), at 30–60% relative humidity, or the hotter-condition charts for 38–49°C (100–120°F), at 15–40% relative humidity.

steps.title: Warm the engine and connect the service unit
steps.body: Run the engine to normal operating temperature, then connect the air-conditioning service unit. Choose the ambient-temperature branch in the [pressure-test procedure](#/document/G1727492).

steps.title: Establish the specified cooling demand
steps.body: Select the lowest temperature, disable dual temperature operation if equipped, set the blower manually to HI, select FRESH air where available and switch A/C on. Open all windows and leave the hood open.

steps.title: Confirm operation and let pressures settle
steps.body: Confirm that the compressor and engine cooling fans are operating or engaged. Let the engine idle until both pressures stabilize or fluctuate within a repeating range.

steps.title: Record and compare both pressures
steps.body: Record shop temperature, discharge pressure and suction pressure. For fluctuating readings, record the average. Compare each pressure with its corresponding chart; the attached illustration is only the lower-temperature discharge chart.

steps.title: Follow the pressure pattern to the next check
steps.body: Use the findings below to guide diagnosis. Before replacing a variable compressor, recover and recharge the system to the vehicle specification, then retest above 70°F. Keep that requirement separate from the general minimum test temperature.

watchFor.title: Other reasons for inadequate compressor operation
watchFor.body: Consider a loose drive belt, slipping clutch, an open or shorted clutch coil or loose mounting, dirty or sticking switch contacts, circuit resistance, an open circuit or blown fuse, and engine-computer interruption.

watchFor.title: Contributors to compressor damage
watchFor.body: The diagnostic table also identifies incorrect clutch air gap, a blocked suction-accumulator refrigerant-oil bleed hose and refrigerant leaks.

notes: Rear-door and rear-hatch opening directions apply only to body configurations with those openings.
A pressure pattern identifies possible causes; it does not establish that a particular component has failed.

diagnostics.finding: High discharge pressure with normal-to-high suction pressure.
diagnostics.meaning: Possible inadequate condenser airflow or engine overheating.
diagnostics.next: Investigate airflow and engine temperature.

diagnostics.finding: Normal-to-high discharge pressure with normal suction pressure.
diagnostics.meaning: Possible refrigerant overcharge or air in the refrigerant.
diagnostics.next: Investigate charge condition.

diagnostics.finding: Normal-to-low discharge pressure with high suction pressure.
diagnostics.meaning: Possible low compressor performance.
diagnostics.next: Apply the charge-and-retest requirement before condemning a variable compressor.

diagnostics.finding: Normal-to-low discharge pressure with normal-to-high suction pressure.
diagnostics.meaning: A suction-line restriction downstream of the service access valve is possible.
diagnostics.next: Investigate the suction line and restriction location.

diagnostics.finding: Normal-to-low discharge pressure with low suction pressure.
diagnostics.meaning: Possible low charge from leakage, or a suction-line restriction upstream of the service access valve.
diagnostics.next: Distinguish leakage from restriction.

diagnostics.finding: Erratic operation or no compressor operation.
diagnostics.meaning: Possible poor connections at the ambient-air-temperature sensor, pressure transducer or evaporator-temperature sensor, or low charge from leakage.
diagnostics.next: Check these possibilities before selecting a replacement component.

verification.title: Keep a usable test record
verification.body: Record ambient temperature, both pressures, whether averages were used, the selected chart range and whether each result was within its normal band.

verification.title: Document any required retest
verification.body: For variable-compressor assessment, record the results after recovery and correct recharging, with the retest performed above 70°F.

procedures.purpose: Complete 5.2L refrigerant-pressure test, including both ambient-temperature branches, chart selection and diagnostic decisions.

guides.title: Replace the A/C compressor on 2.3L, 3.7L, 5.0L or 5.2L engines
guides.summary: Replace the compressor using the correct engine-specific access, contamination treatment, seals and fastening procedure.
guides.introduction: The air conditioning (A/C) compressor circulates refrigerant through the cooling system, helping the climate controls cool and dehumidify cabin air. Replacement involves opening the refrigerant circuit, removing the belt-driven compressor and restoring its connections and lubrication.
guides.why: An internally failed compressor can leave contamination that damages its replacement. Clean openings, correct oil and new seals protect the repaired system. Mounting arrangements also differ: the 5.2L requires new studbolts, while other engines have their own tightening instructions.

when.summary: When compressor replacement is required, including contamination treatment after an internal failure.
notes: Poor cooling alone does not establish that the compressor needs replacement.

prepare.title: Arrange refrigerant servicing
prepare.detail: Have refrigerant recovery, evacuation and charging capability, correct seal lubricant, clean polyalkylene glycol (PAG) oil and suitable port protection.

prepare.title: Prepare the correct variant
prepare.detail: Obtain the engine-specific belt instructions and required seals. Have new compressor studbolts for the 5.2L and torque-angle capability.

prepare.title: Plan underbody access
prepare.detail: The 5.0L procedure specifies a hoist with the transmission in Neutral. Use the designated lifting points; never work beneath jack-only support.

steps.title: Set the contamination repair scope
steps.body: After internal failure, flush the system before installing the replacement if flushing equipment is available. Otherwise, replace all contaminated components after installing the new compressor. Replace the thermostatic expansion valve and receiver drier element as directed by the flushing procedure.

steps.title: Recover refrigerant and remove the drive belt
steps.body: Use the [refrigerant recovery procedure](#/document/G1912323) before opening any lines. Remove the compressor belt using the procedure for the actual engine; belt access and installation must follow that variant.

steps.title: Clear access and disconnect the compressor
steps.body: On the 5.0L, remove the transmission fluid cooler tubes. On the 5.2L, if equipped, remove their bracket nuts and position the tubes aside. Release harness retainers, disconnect electrical connections and detach the refrigerant lines. Protect every open port immediately.

steps.title: Remove the unit and assess supplied accessories
steps.body: Follow the mounting removal in the [2.3L](#/document/G1676736), [3.7L](#/document/G1676738), [5.0L](#/document/G1676740) or [5.2L](#/document/G1727495) procedure. Discard the 5.2L studbolts. If the replacement lacks clutch components, transfer the old disc and hub, pulley and field coil only if suitable for reuse.

steps.title: Prepare seals and lubrication
steps.body: Fit new O-rings; the 3.7L and 5.0L also require new gasket seals and disposal of the removed seals. For the 2.3L and 5.2L, lubricate new O-rings only with the specified material. Follow [Refrigerant Oil Adding](#/document/G1912330) for the correct clean PAG oil quantity.

steps.title: Install with the correct fastening sequence
steps.body: Follow the selected engine procedure, including the illustrated tightening order for the 3.7L and 5.0L. On the 5.2L, loosely install new studbolts so the dowels seat correctly, then tighten in the shown sequence to 18 lb.ft (25 Nm), followed by 90°.

steps.title: Restore connections and refrigerant service
steps.body: Reverse the remaining removal operations, removing protective caps before connecting lines. Restore wiring, belt and any disturbed cooler tubes. Complete evacuation and charging through the [refrigerant service procedure](#/document/G1912323), using its applicable specifications.

watchFor.title: Unprotected openings
watchFor.body: Dirt entering disconnected lines or compressor ports can compromise the replacement.

watchFor.title: Mixed installation instructions
watchFor.body: Do not apply the 5.2L torque-angle method or another engine's mounting sequence across variants.

notes: Receiver drier replacement is not routine for every A/C repair; physical contamination from compressor failure or drier damage changes that decision.

diagnostics.finding: Internal compressor failure with contamination
diagnostics.meaning: Replacing the compressor alone leaves a cause of repeat damage.
diagnostics.next: Complete the flushing or contaminated-component replacement branch.

verification.title: Confirm installation requirements
verification.body: Check that new seals, correct oil addition and the engine-specific fastening sequence have been completed.

verification.title: Record the completed repair
verification.body: Record the engine variant, contamination treatment, oil addition and refrigerant servicing results.

Determine and add the required refrigerant-system oil.
